Human Agent

Agents: the full docs are one file at /llms-full.txt. This page as markdown: /agents.md.

pragma, for your agent

Everything an agent needs to build with pragma, in files it reads without a browser. Human: copy the prompt, paste it into your coding agent and say what to build.

The prompt

Replace the brackets with your app. The agent reads the docs, installs pragma, creates the app and runs pragma check --strict until it passes.

Read https://pragma.leonavas.com/llms-full.txt and create a pragma app that [describe your app]. Install pragma if missing, or validate the version with pragma -V and .pragma/version and run pragma self-update and pragma upgrade if outdated. Follow the AGENTS.md that pragma new writes into the app, and finish with pragma check --strict at zero errors and zero warnings.

Install and create

One Rust binary. On Linux and macOS, run the installer. On Windows, download the binary from GitHub Releases. On other platforms, build from source with Cargo. Node 22 or newer only runs .server.js files.

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leonavas/pragma/main/install.sh | sh
pragma new my-app
cd my-app
pragma dev

Validate version and update

Validate the pragma version before you change code:

  • Run pragma -V to check the installed CLI version.
  • Compare that version with .pragma/version inside the app.
  • Run pragma self-update to update the CLI binary from GitHub Releases if the CLI is old.
  • Run pragma upgrade inside the app to update .pragma/ (runtime, docs, base.css, version) if .pragma/ is outdated.
pragma -V
cat .pragma/version
pragma self-update
pragma upgrade

Files for agents

Same content as the HTML pages, in markdown. No hidden text, nothing written only for agents.

  • /llms-full.txt: the app rules and every doc in one file. Start here.
  • /llms.txt: the index, in the llmstxt.org format.
  • /index.md: the landing page.
  • /agents.md: this page.

A request for / or /agents with Accept: text/markdown gets the markdown file instead of the HTML. One doc per file:

  • /docs/rules.md: the rules of every app (AGENTS.md). Read first.
  • /docs/structure.md: where each file goes, pragma.json.
  • /docs/syntax.md: HTML directives and blocks.
  • /docs/components.md: components, props, slots.
  • /docs/state.md: script, actions, derived values, stores.
  • /docs/routes.md: pages, router, head tags.
  • /docs/data.md: load, server actions, SSR.
  • /docs/overlays.md: modal, alert, dropdown.
  • /docs/css.md: styles and theme.
  • /docs/classes.md: every utility class.
  • /docs/webmcp.md: forms as agent tools, markdown for agents.
  • /docs/packages.md: npm packages.
  • /docs/performance.md: defaults and the size report.
  • /docs/logs.md: OpenTelemetry logs.
  • /docs/cli.md: commands and check rules.

WebMCP tools on this site

This page and the landing page expose these tools to agents in the browser, as declarative WebMCP forms. Humans use the same forms. The landing page also has add_task (its demo to-do list), and /examples/data has sign_guestbook.

routes/examples/components/index.html:
One file: script, markup and style

A top-level let is state, export let is a prop, a function is an action or a derived value, and {$count} puts a value in the text.

  • export let start = 0 declares a prop with a default. The default's type converts the attribute: start="10" arrives as the number 10, so no Number() anywhere. Props are read-only: let count = start copies one into state.
  • const atMinimum = () => … is a derived value: used in a binding (:disabled="$atMinimum"), it runs on every render. In JS you call it: atMinimum().
  • function increase(event) is an action when an event names it. Without parentheses, @click="increase" passes the DOM event, here to read event.shiftKey. Assigning count schedules one render per microtask; there is no setState and no this.
  • With parentheses the function gets only what you list: paths, literals, event and el, the element that has the @. Reset hides itself after a click, so @click="reset(el)" moves the focus to + and keyboard users keep their place.
  • A store function works the same way, with no wrapper: @click="shared.cart.add(product)". A component that only reads and calls a store needs no script, as on the stores page.
  • <style> is scoped by the build: .counter-step only matches inside this component, with no added specificity, so write plain selectors. :global(…) opts out only what is inside it (:global(html[data-theme="dark"]) .counter-step is still this component's buttons), and the root itself is [data-c="counter"]. A separate counter.css works the same way; having both it and the <style> (or a <script> and a counter.js) is a check error (html/duplicate-module).

The component lives in _components/counter/ next to this page, so it is used as <p-counter>. Moving the folder to lib/components/ would make it <c-counter> for every route.

Copy what you change (let rows = files.map(file => ({ ...file }))) or ask the owner to change it. The page script reads the loader's result with import { data } from 'pragma'.

No script: build-time props, class and slot fallback

A component without a script is fully expanded at build and ships zero JavaScript.

caller text

Without a script, {$label} is replaced by the caller's text at build time. A bare attribute like active is truthy; a missing one, "" and "false" are falsy. class on the tag is appended to the root's classes.

Typed props: the default decides the type

An attribute is always text; export let converts it with the type of its default.
  • A number default turns "5" into 5. A boolean default turns a bare attribute or "true" into true and "false" into false. A string default keeps the text. Any other default (an object, null) takes the value as passed with :prop="path".
  • A missing attribute gives the default. HTML (<if $locked>) and JS (locked) read the same converted value.
  • An attribute the script does not declare is an error at the call site (html/unknown-prop), and assigning a prop is js/prop-write.

Where a component lives decides its tag

Every component on this page sits in routes/examples/components/_components/, so it is a <p-…> visible to this folder and the folders below it. The lookup walks up from the page folder to routes/, so routes/_components/x/ is visible to every route. lib/components/x/ makes it <c-x> everywhere; promoting one is a move plus a rename from p- to c-.

  • p- names are private to their folder, styles included. This page and the syntax page each have their own <p-badge>; the build gives each one its own data-c and scopes each <style> to it, so both write .badge-icon and never share a rule.
  • A <p-x> used outside routes/ is an error, and so are two components with the same folder name on one page (<c-card> plus <p-card>).
  • A component cannot have a .server.js: its data comes from the page's load, as in the list above.
  • A component cannot use itself, and its root cannot be <template>, <slot> or another component.
  • A component's script loads only on pages that use it. Its <style> goes into the single app stylesheet, scoped by its data-c.

routes/examples/data/index.html:
load() with a skeleton

load() runs on the server, and its return value is data: {data.loadedAt} in HTML, data.products in a script. Switch categories to watch the skeleton.

load receives { params, query, request, env, log }. The build adds a script to <head> that starts GET /_data/<path>?<query> before any module loads, and the page shows the <if page.loading> branch until it resolves. Every navigation, including a query change, runs load again. The page's own <script> only derives which category link is current from query.

The prebuilt HTML carries the loading chain as an inert template: the skeleton appears once the boot script runs, while content outside the chain, like the category links, is visible immediately. request is the Fetch Request (headers, cookies); env holds the Workers bindings, and on Node it is process.env. Using data.* on a page without a load fails check.

Helpers whose name starts with _ and ends in .server.js are private to the folder and never reach the browser; JSON is imported with with { type: 'json' }. A client module that imports a .server.js file fails pragma check with js/import, and node:* imports are allowed only in server files.

A form backed by a server action

Writes go through call('sign', input), imported from 'pragma', which runs actions.sign in the page's .server.js.

@submit calls preventDefault() for you, then sign() sends a POST /_action/<current path>/sign with a JSON body. data is live: assigning data.guestbook re-renders the list. A non-2xx response makes call throw with the server message, which the component keeps in its let error.

call works from a component too and always targets the current page's .server.js: this guestbook calls routes/examples/data/index.server.js. A server action may return a raw Response to pick the status, here a 422 for invalid input. Actions also receive query and request.

The endpoint answers 404 for an unknown action, 400 for a body that is not JSON and 405 for anything but POST. Actions are the only write path: there are no /api routes and no GET endpoints, so nothing can serve RSS, a sitemap or raw JSON dynamically.

ssr = true: data in the first HTML

With export const ssr = true in the .server.js, the server renders the page with its data, so the skeleton never appears. Reload the frame and the counts arrive already in the HTML.

The line must be literally export const ssr = true. The server runs load, renders the page into <main data-page>, every {data.x} included, and appends the data as <script type="application/json" id="pragma-data">. The client binds to that HTML without re-rendering and without a second fetch. The response is text/html with cache-control: private, no-cache, HEAD works, and a client-side navigation to an SSR route fetches the rendered HTML from the server instead of the prebuilt file.

The page's script and its components' scripts also run on the server, once per request, so their initial lets, props and derived values are in the first HTML too. mount() runs only in the browser: $hydratedAt is empty in the HTML and gets the time when the page boots. A script that reads window, document, localStorage or a store while it runs is left to the browser, and the rest of the page still renders. Head tags take {} too, but only with SSR: this route writes <title>{data.votes} votes · SSR demo</title> and the same in og:title, so link previews see the live count (SEO and head).

When load throws

An error thrown in load reaches the page as page.error.

The response is HTTP 500 with {"error":{"message"}}, an ERROR log on the server, and {page.error.message} on the client, rendered by the <else-if page.error> branch. Content outside the loading chain, like the filter links, keeps working. "Not found" is not an error: return { product: null } and render it.

routes/examples/logs/index.html:
log in page and component scripts

Import log from 'pragma' in any page, component or store script and call debug, info, warn or error from an action or mount(). Keep the message short and fixed and put the variable parts in attributes named like OpenTelemetry's (order.id, exception.message), so records group and filter cleanly.

The runtime adds url.path, a timestamp and the page's traceId, queues the record and posts batches to /_otel. In pragma dev every call also prints to the browser console, and the dev server prints each received record as a JSON line in the terminal. debug stays in the console: the client sends info and above.

What is logged without asking

An action that throws or rejects is not swallowed: the error reaches window, and the runtime logs it as ERROR with exception.type, exception.message and exception.stacktrace. The same goes for any uncaught error or unhandled rejection on the page. Do not wrap code in try/catch only to log it again.

  • navigation (info): every client navigation, with pragma.route, push or pop, and duration_ms.
  • navigation failed and loader failed (error): a page module or a load request that failed.
  • A traceparent header on every runtime fetch (/_data, /_action), so server records join the client trace.
  • On the server, one record per request: GET /orders with method, route, status and duration in seconds; ERROR for 5xx.

log in load and server actions

load and every server action receive log in their argument. Its records carry the request's traceId and spanId, taken from the client's traceparent. A server action that throws is logged with its stack, answers 500, and call() rejects with the message on the client. pragma dev also prints server log.debug; in production it is off unless PRAGMA_LOG_LEVEL=debug.

Logging from utils/

The services from 'pragma' belong to page, component and store scripts. A plain module in utils/ imports the same client logger from .pragma/log.js; its records join the same batches and the same trace.

import { log } from '../.pragma/log.js'

const euro = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IE', { style: 'currency', currency: 'EUR' })

export function formatPrice(cents) {
  if (!Number.isInteger(cents)) log.warn('price is not in cents', { 'price.value': String(cents) })
  return euro.format(cents / 100)
}

Where the records go

Client batches and server records meet at the server: /_otel accepts batches up to 256 KB and forwards them with the server's own records. Everything is configured with the standard OpenTelemetry environment variables, so any OTLP/HTTP collector works.

OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=https://otel.example.com OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS=x-api-key=secret node dist/server/node.mjs

Never log passwords, tokens, cookies, emails or other personal data, never log inside loops or on every keystroke, and never use console.*: pragma check rejects it with js/console. On a static host there is no /_otel: the client stops sending after the first 404 or 405, while pragma serve always accepts it.

routes/examples/overlays/index.html:
Modal with @open and @close

@open="about-pragma" opens the overlay with that id and @close closes the one it sits in; neither needs a line of JS. <c-modal> takes id and title, a default slot and an actions slot. It closes on Esc, a click on the backdrop, the × button, any @close, and the browser's Back button.

Alert with await confirm(id)

import { confirm } from 'pragma', then await confirm(id) opens the alert and resolves with the value of the @close button that was clicked, or 'cancel' on Esc and Back. <c-alert> is a <dialog role="alertdialog">, so a backdrop click does not dismiss it. For a destructive action, put autofocus on the safe button.

Dropdown on the popover API

<c-dropdown> is a [popover] under its button, flipped above when there is no room below. It closes on an outside click, Esc, @close and Back, and it does not lock scroll. Items can combine @close with @click, and pass arguments: @click="sortBy('size')".

The label here is a dynamic prop, :label="$menuLabel": the dropdown has no script, so it reads the caller's derived function on every render.

Stacking, open and close

Overlays stack: Discard with an edited name opens an alert on top of the modal. Each open overlay pushes a history entry, so Back closes only the top one. Focus returns to whatever opened each layer, and the page behind stops scrolling while a modal or alert is open, with the scrollbar gutter reserved only if there was a scrollbar.

From a script, open(id) and close(id) from 'pragma' do what @open and @close do. Open overlays only in response to a user action, and never keep "is open" in state: the <dialog> already knows.

They are ordinary components

The three overlays ship in the starter as lib/components/modal, alert and dropdown: one .html each, with no script, that you can restyle like any other component. The behavior lives in .pragma/overlay.js, which the build adds only to pages that contain a <dialog> or [popover].

  • Do not create a <dialog> or [popover] by hand, call showModal(), use window.confirm or role="menu", or import .pragma/overlay.js yourself.

Any package manager works: pragma reads package.json and node_modules/. A client import must be listed under dependencies, use a quoted specifier and name what it takes. These are the three packages this page runs.

npm i valibot es-toolkit dayjs --ignore-scripts

found 0 vulnerabilities
grep -A6 dependencies package.json

    "dayjs": "^1.11.23",
    "es-toolkit": "^1.53.2",
    "highlight.js": "^11.12.0",
    "valibot": "^1.5.0"
  }

Each package becomes one file, /assets/npm/<package>-<hash>.js (@date-fns/tz turns into date-fns__tz), and code shared between packages goes to /assets/npm/_*.js. Pages that import it get a modulepreload for it. process.env.NODE_ENV is replaced with "production" in builds and "development" in dev.

Tree shaking, measured: highlight.js on this site

The code blocks on this site are colored by highlight.js. Importing the package index pulls in all 193 languages. Importing highlight.js/lib/core plus the three grammars the site needs is 95% less gzip: the 190 unused language modules are dropped. The core itself is not shaken: its ESM entry re-exports CommonJS, and CommonJS ships whole.

The smallest chunk is the one the browser never loads. Every showcase tokenizes in load: _source.server.js runs highlight.js on Node and sends each line with its color ranges, the section pages use ssr = true, and the mount(el) of c-showcase paints the ranges with the CSS Custom Highlight API. The code is in the first HTML and gets its colors when the component mounts, with no extra download. The client chunk exists only for the SEO page's response view, which loads it with import(); lazy chunks are not preloaded and do not count in the page size.

Named imports: only what you use ships

valibot is pure ESM with one module per function, the best case for tree shaking. This form imports eight names and ships 1.35 kB gzip of valibot. The schema is a constant in the <script>; validation is a derived function, so {$status} reruns it on every keystroke without any wiring.

Subpath imports share one chunk

groupBy comes from the es-toolkit index and debounce from es-toolkit/function. Both end up in a single es-toolkit-*.js of 0.43 kB gzip. The same two helpers from lodash cost 6.49 kB, because CommonJS cannot be shaken.

The debounced function just assigns two let variables: a timer firing outside an action still renders, because state is a reactive Proxy. mount() returns a cleanup that cancels a pending call when the component leaves the page.

CommonJS, loaded with import() after a click

dayjs is CommonJS, so the core and the relativeTime plugin ship whole: 3.69 kB gzip. When a package is only needed after an interaction, await import() it inside the action. The chunk is left out of the modulepreload list and the page size, and the first paint does not wait for it.

import('pkg') always brings the whole package, so keep it for code you need all of anyway. The default export of a CommonJS module arrives as default.

What common packages cost

Gzip size of the /assets/npm/ file for each import, measured with pragma build on the packages test app in core/cli/xtask/packages/app. The runtime alone is 8.7 kB gzip per page, so a large package like chart.js belongs behind an import().

Prefer the platform first: Intl for dates, numbers and plurals, fetch, crypto.randomUUID(), structuredClone. Avoid moment, lodash, axios, uuid, nanoid and anything that builds HTML.

routes/examples/routing/index.html:
Files are routes

The path of a file under routes/ is its URL. index.html maps to the folder, [name] in a file or folder name is a param, and a static segment beats a param: demo/new.html wins over demo/[slug].html for /demo/new. A page is a fragment with optional top-level <title>, <meta> and <link> tags; it has no <html>, <head> or <body>.

FileURL
routes/index.html/
routes/about.html/about
routes/blog/index.html/blog
routes/blog/[slug].html/blog/:slug
routes/blog/[slug]/edit.html/blog/:slug/edit
routes/[lang]/index.html/:lang

Names starting with _ are private; only _layout.html and _404.html are special, any other _x.html is an error. x.html next to x/index.html, or two params in the same folder, is app/route-conflict. There is no [...rest] and no optional param. Subfolders can define nested layouts with routes/<dir>/_layout.html and <slot></slot>.

Dynamic routes with [slug]

The param is params.slug everywhere: in HTML, in the page's <script> after import { params } from 'pragma', and in a load. It is always a URL-decoded string. Reading a param the route does not have is a check error that lists the valid ones. Here a derived function in the page's script finds the post in a local module; with a .server.js the same lookup would run in load (see Data and SSR).

A missing post is data, not an error: the branch renders "not found" and the status stays 200, a soft 404. On static hosting something has to map /demo/abc to [slug].html; pragma serve, the Node adapter and the Workers adapter do it from the manifest.

Route-local components

A component in _components/ next to a route is used as <p-name> by every page in that folder and below: the lookup walks up from the page to routes/. p-post-meta has no <script>, so :post="$post" aliases the page's path at build time and {$post.author} reads through it. Promoting it means moving the folder to lib/components/ and renaming it c-post-meta.

Layouts and automatic active links

routes/_layout.html wraps every page. Its optional <head> comes first, is static (a binding there fails check with html/head) and is copied into every page; exactly one <main data-page> holds a lone <slot>. Subfolders can add a nested routes/<dir>/_layout.html with a <slot></slot> to wrap every page in that folder inside the parent layout. The layout has no <script> and reads only shared, params and query; behavior goes in a component. A <title> in the layout <head> is the fallback for pages without one, and pragma.json's name is the last resort. A page can also write <meta> and <link> at its top level: the build moves them into <head>, replacing the layout's tag with the same name (see SEO and head).

Any routed <a href> without query or hash that points to the current page gets aria-current="page", in the prebuilt HTML and after every navigation. This site styles .nav-link[aria-current="page"] in green: look at the header above, or at the demo nav in any frame on this page.

Tabs and filters live in the query

query.tab holds the query as a string, in HTML and in scripts (import { query } from 'pragma'); a repeated key keeps the last value, and a missing query.x never throws. Links build their URL with href="?tab={tab.id}". Since automatic aria-current ignores links with a query, bind :aria-current to a derived value that is 'true' or false.

Every navigation, including a query-only one, recreates the page state: click the counter, then switch tabs, and it starts again at zero.

Navigating from an action, and full reloads

After an action, navigate(url) from 'pragma' goes through the router like a link click. Use it only when there is no link to click: never a <button> that navigates, location.href or history.pushState. A link with data-reload, target or download, or a click with a modifier key, skips the router and loads the page in full.

The 404 page

A URL that matches no route renders routes/_404.html, served with status 404 by pragma serve and the Node adapter. It is a normal fragment with a <title>; it may have a <script> for state and actions, but never a .server.js. The Workers adapter resolves param routes and answers unknown URLs with this page and a real 404 too.

What the router does for free

  • Intercepts same-origin <a href> clicks and swaps only <main data-page> plus the page's <title>, <meta> and <link> tags, so description, canonical and Open Graph follow the page (SEO and head). The layout stays mounted and its directives are reapplied.
  • Prefetches on hover, on focus and when a link scrolls into view (at idle): the prebuilt HTML plus a modulepreload of the route's modules, which downloads and compiles them without running them until you navigate.
  • Wraps the swap in document.startViewTransition where the browser has it.
  • Scrolls to the top on a new page, restores the position on back and forward, scrolls to #hash targets and moves focus to <main>.

None of it needs code: there is no router to configure, and the pages on this site use nothing else.

Layout defaults, page overrides

A tag at the top level of a page replaces the layout tag with the same name, property, http-equiv or rel + hreflang, in place; a tag the layout lacks, like canonical, is appended. <html lang> comes from lang in pragma.json, and charset and viewport are always emitted.

Keep canonical and og:url out of the layout, or every page claims the same address. X reads og:title, og:description and og:image when the twitter:* versions are missing, so this site's layout sets only twitter:card, and a page overrides og:* once for both. Add a twitter:* tag only when X should show something else, like the shorter title on this demo page.

Tags from server data with ssr = true

Write {data.post.title} inside <title>, and :content, :href or {} in an attribute of <meta> and <link>, reading data, params or query; then add export const ssr = true to the route's .server.js. The server fills them before it sends the page, so a link-preview bot, which never runs JavaScript, sees the article instead of the site defaults.

Build absolute URLs in load from a fixed origin, never from the request's Host header. A missing value keeps the static fallback, such as the <title> text; a <meta> left without content or a <link> without href is dropped. On client navigation the router replaces <title>, <meta> and <link> with the next page's.

Soft 404 and real 404

load returns data, not a status, so a dynamic route whose entity is missing still answers 200: a soft 404, which search engines may index as an empty page. Bind <meta name="robots"> to data.head.robots and return 'noindex' only for the missing entity; in every other case the value is undefined and the tag is dropped.

An address that matches no route gets routes/_404.html with status 404, from pragma serve, the Node adapter and Workers alike.

robots.txt and a sitemap

Files in public/ are served from the site root as they are, with the right content-type. Routes only produce HTML, so sitemap.xml is a static file too: write it by hand, or generate it from your data with a script before pragma build, and point to it from robots.txt with a Sitemap: line.

Structured data with JSON-LD

Write one <script type="application/ld+json"> per schema at the top level of the page. The build moves it into <head> and rejects invalid JSON with the line and column. Inside its strings, {data.article.title} works as it does in a <meta>: with ssr = true the server writes each value JSON-escaped, so a quote in a title cannot break the script. JSON-LD without {} is static and needs no ssr.

routes/examples/state/index.html:
A page's script

Every top-level let is state, read as $visitor in HTML; every top-level function is reachable from HTML too.

{$greeting}

{$greeting} calls greeting() on every render, and @click="forget" calls forget(). A page writes its script as a <script> at the top of its .html, or as a .js with the same name; this page uses index.js because its .html is the whole article. A name in HTML that the script does not declare fails check with html/unknown-name.

Derived values are functions

Anything computed from state is a function, called again on every render, so there is nothing to keep in sync.

HTML only reads paths, never formulas, so the template asks for $perPersonLabel and the script computes it. Inside the script you call them like any function: total() reads bill() and tip(). :model keeps the input's type: a number field writes a number, or null when it is empty. Never keep a derived copy in a let that actions update.

Actions take arguments

An event calls a function by name, and inside a <for> it passes the item: @change="toggle(job)".

State is a deep proxy: job.done = true, jobs.push(…) and jobs = jobs.filter(…) all render. Arguments can be paths (job, $draft, data.x), simple literals, event or el, never expressions. An async action renders when its first part returns ("Saving…") and again after each await; renders are batched per microtask.

Props: export let, typed by the default

export let used = 0 declares a prop, and the default's type converts the attribute text.

used="72" arrives as the number 72 because the default is a number; a bare critical is true and "false" is false; a missing prop keeps its default, so the second meter's total is 100. Props are read-only: assigning one fails check with js/prop-write, so copy it into a let to change it (let count = start). That goes deep: in dev, writing into an object prop (item.done = true) throws an error that names the prop; copy it first (let draft = { ...item }). A prop the script does not declare fails at the call site with html/unknown-prop. More in Components.

mount() and its cleanup

function mount() runs once after the first render and returns the cleanup.

It is only for external effects: timers, window or document listeners, observers. mount runs only in the browser, so it is also where browser-only reads belong: the clock reads window.innerWidth there, not at the top of the script, because on an SSR page the script also runs on the server. mount(el) receives the component's root element for an observer or a measurement; read from it, never write to it. The cleanup runs when the owner leaves the DOM; for a page, on navigation. An async function mount() works too: the runtime awaits it and uses the function it resolves to as the cleanup, even when the owner left before it resolved. Never fetch data in mount; that is what load is for.

Timers and promises just assign

A callback that runs later assigns the let like an action does, and the page renders.

The action starts the interval and mount only returns the cleanup that stops it. Maps, Sets, Dates and class instances are not tracked: assign a new value instead of changing them in place.

event, el and services from 'pragma'

A handler without parentheses receives the DOM event: @keydown="inspectKey" calls inspectKey(event). With parentheses it receives only what it lists, and two names are always there: event and el, the element that has the directive. Everything else a script needs comes from import { … } from 'pragma'.

Use el instead of an id lookup or event.currentTarget, which is the root the runtime listens on, not your element. The services are shared (stores), data (the load result), params, query, page, log, call (server actions), navigate and open, close, confirm (overlays). Read data and the route inside functions, never at the top level of the script. Never write to the DOM: read event, change state and let the bindings follow.

Script mistakes that check catches

Four mistakes run without an error in the browser and show a wrong or stale value. pragma check stops each one and names the fix. This is real output for one page script:

   |                ^
routes/orders.html:6:7 error [js/stale-derived] `label` reads `discount` once, when the script starts, and never updates: make it a function (`const label = () => discount + '% off'`) and use `$label` in HTML, `label()` in JS; or assign it in an action to change it
 6 |   let label = discount + '% off'
   |       ^
routes/orders.html:9:26 error [js/derived-call] `empty` is a function (a derived value): call it in JS: `empty()` (`$empty` without `()` is only for HTML)
 9 |   const summary = () => (empty ? 'No orders' : orders.length + ' orders')
   |                          ^
routes/orders.html:12:5 error [js/dollar-in-script] `$orders` is HTML only; in <script> write `orders`
 12 |     $orders = []
    |     ^
4 error(s), 0 warning(s)
  • js/top-level-data: data is undefined until the loader ends, so read it in a function: const orders = () => data.orders.
  • js/stale-derived: a let computed from another let or a prop is computed once. Make it a function, as in Derived values.
  • js/derived-call: in JS a derived value is a call, empty(); empty alone is the function, which is always truthy.
  • js/dollar-in-script: $ is HTML only. In the script every name is plain.

Coming from state(ctx)

  • export const state = () => ({ count: 0 }) is now let count = 0; getters are functions.
  • export const actions is now top-level functions, and ctx.scope.item is an argument: @click="remove(item)".
  • ctx.update(fn) is gone: assign the let. ctx.$.prop is export let prop.
  • ctx.data, ctx.call, ctx.log and the rest come from 'pragma'; :text is {path} inside the element.

The old API fails check with js/legacy-api, and each message names the replacement.

The store restores the listed values when its module loads and writes them back after each render. It also listens to the storage event, so every other tab of the same origin follows live: type in either textarea, then reload the page. Persist preferences, drafts and local-only data, never anything the server owns. persist is the only export a store may have.

A store read only from a script

A derived function can read a store, and it runs again on every render.

p-shipping never mentions the cart in its HTML: remaining() calls shared.cart.total() and the HTML shows {$message}. In a script, a store's derived values are functions you call; in HTML they are paths. Utilities, variants and what check rejects

The card below is styled only with utilities. Variants are hover:, focus:, focus-visible:, active:, disabled:, group-hover:, dark: and the breakpoints sm: to 2xl:; they combine (md:hover:bg-primary-600), and colors take an opacity (bg-accent/20). The palette is white, black, transparent, current and the scales neutral, primary, danger, success, warning in shades 50 to 950, and the full list is .pragma/docs/classes.md.

Anything else is a check error, not a silent no-op: arbitrary values, negative utilities, unknown classes such as shadow-inner, and style="…". The other tabs show the output.

Tokens generate utilities

Each --color-<name> or --color-<name>-<shade> in @layer tokens becomes bg-, text-, border- and the other color utilities. These swatches use this site's own tokens; redefining --color-primary-* rebrands every primary utility at once. The starter ships theme-aware bg-surface, text-ink, text-muted, border-line and the classes .card, .btn, .btn-primary, .btn-danger, .dialog.

The redefinable tokens are --color-*, --font-sans, --font-serif, --font-mono, --radius-*, --shadow-* and --spacing. A new font name such as --font-display does not create font-display. .pragma/base.css also reads --page-bg, --page-fg and --skeleton-bg, which switch in dark mode, plus --container-* for the max-w-* sizes.

Component CSS, scoped by the build

A component's <style> is for what utilities cannot say: here, :has(:checked) drives the selected segment and a custom property that sets the row padding, with no JavaScript at all. Write plain selectors: the build scopes each one to the component.

  • The build marks the root with data-c and adds a :where(…) that matches the root and everything inside it to the last part of every selector, as the app.css tab shows: .density-option:hover or even li never styles anything outside the component, and the scope adds no specificity.
  • Only the last part is scoped, so an outside ancestor needs nothing special: html[data-theme="dark"] .density-option still matches only this component's options.
  • The root is [data-c="density"], and a selector that names it stays as written. :global(…) opts out only what is inside it: .density-rows :global(.hit) keeps .density-rows scoped and lets .hit match anything inside it, child components included. A selector that is all :global, such as :global(:root) { --row-pad: 1rem; }, is global.
  • A page's <style> is scoped to its <main data-page> the same way. All of it goes into @layer components of the single app stylesheet; a separate density.css works the same, and having both is a check error.
  • For a p- component the build makes the scope unique per folder (density-97d4f0 in the tab), so two private components with the same name never share a rule. Forbidden: !important, ID selectors and external @import.

Dynamic styles: .name toggles and data-*

There is no :class and no style: every class name is written out in the source, so check can validate it and the build can generate it. Toggle a class on a condition with .text-accent="$passed". When the value itself varies, bind a data-* attribute (:data-status="$status") and style each value with an attribute selector in the component's <style>. Only the bound form is allowed: a hand-written data-status="ok" fails check with html/data-attribute.

Light and dark theme

Dark mode keys off data-theme="dark": tokens redefined under [data-theme="dark"] switch on their own, and palette colors pair with dark: (bg-white dark:bg-neutral-900), which matches the element or any ancestor. In an app, setTheme() from .pragma/theme.js sets it on <html> and saves it, as the theme-switch.html tab shows; importing that module also adds an inline script that restores the choice, or follows prefers-color-scheme, before first paint.

This site is dark only, so the live box sets data-theme on its own root to keep the switch inside the box. Without the .pragma/theme.js import, dark mode never activates: there is no media-query fallback. The import may also be written in the absolute form '/.pragma/theme.js'.

Text: {path}

{$name} is the only way to put a value in text, and it works inside attribute strings too: title="Profile of {$name}", href="#user-{$slug}".

  • Only paths go between the braces: $x, data.x, shared.cart.total, params.id or a <for> variable. A function from the script is a derived value: {$length} calls length() on every render.
  • Values are escaped; null and undefined print nothing. A page with ssr gets them in the first HTML; otherwise the runtime fills them at boot, and the raw {…} never shows.
  • Braces are literal text inside <code> and <pre>, which is how this page shows them. Anywhere else, \{ writes a literal brace.
  • For a whole value or a boolean attribute use :attr instead (:disabled="$offline"). {} is not allowed in class (use .name) or in a component prop (pass a path: :title="$title").

Values are paths, never expressions

Every directive takes a path of the form root.a.b. The roots are $x (a name from the owner's script: state, prop, constant or function), data (the load result), shared.store, params, query, page.loading / page.error and the variable of an enclosing <for>. Properties work, so $items.length is fine; calls, indexes and operators are not.

The only operator is !, and only in <if>, <else-if>, :show and .class. Anything derived (a total, a label, an aria-* string) is a function in the script, const total = () => …, which is what every example below does.

Bindings: :attr, :aria-*, :data-*

:href, :title, :disabled or any other :attr sets the whole attribute: false, null and undefined remove it, true sets it empty. Toggle the switch: while the service is down the link has no href at all.

aria-* states need the strings 'true' / 'false', because boolean false removes the attribute. :data-tone is the hook for a style with many values: the component's CSS selects [data-tone="ok"] without touching classes. Only the bound form is allowed; a hand-written data-tone="ok" fails check with html/data-attribute.

Class toggles: .class and .class="!v"

.line-through="$done" adds the class while the value is truthy; .is-pending="!$done" does the opposite. The class must be a known utility or a class from the project's CSS, and variants work: .md:font-semibold only bolds from 48rem up. Static classes on the same element are left alone.

There is no :class and no {} inside class: both are check errors (html/class), because a computed class name could never be generated into the CSS. Write the static classes in class and toggle each optional one; for a value with many states, bind :data-tone and style the attribute, as the bindings example does.

:show hides, <if> creates

:show toggles the hidden attribute, so the element, its listeners and its input state stay in the DOM. <if> inserts and removes its content. An element with autofocus inside a block that was just inserted receives focus, so opening the right pane puts the caret in its input.

Two-way binding with :model

:model works on input, select and textarea, and only with a $x or shared.x path. The value keeps its type: checkboxes are booleans, radios hold the value of the checked one, number and range give a number (or null when the field is empty), everything else a string. A prop cannot be the target (js/prop-write).

Events: event by default, el on request

@keydown="pressed" calls the script's function with the DOM event, so function pressed(event) needs no wrapper. With parentheses the function receives only what is listed: @focusout="record('@focusout', 'field lost focus')", @change="toggle(item)", @dblclick="doubled(el, event)". el is the element that has the directive.

  • An argument is a path (item, $draft, data.x), a string in quotes, a number, true, false, null, event or el. Expressions are a check error.
  • Double-click the bold word: event.target is the <strong>, el is still the <p>. Use el instead of an id lookup; event.currentTarget is the root the runtime listens on.
  • A store function is a handler too, with no wrapper in the script: @click="shared.cart.remove(line)" (Stores).
  • @submit calls preventDefault() for you, so the form never reloads the page.
  • The same function can be an action and a helper: record runs from @focusout and from the other functions.

Overlay shortcuts: @open and bare @close

@open="id" opens the overlay with that id and @close, written without a value, closes the overlay around it. The button's value becomes the result of confirm(id); the overlays section covers modal, alert and dropdown in depth.

Conditions: <if>, <else-if>, <else>

The path in a block tag is unquoted: <if $loading>, <else-if $noOrders>. Any number of <else-if> may follow, and each one must come right after the closing tag of the previous branch. Every block holds exactly one root element, which carries the directives; the block tag itself takes none.

Lists: <for> with key, and <empty>

<for item in group.items key=item.id> repeats its root element; the key is required, starts with the loop variable and must be unique (duplicates throw in dev). Updates diff by key. <empty> right after </for> renders when the list is empty.

Pass the item to the function: @change="toggle(item)", @click="clear(group)". State is a deep proxy, so item.done = !item.done and group.items = [] render without copying anything. A loop variable cannot shadow a root such as data or page.

Static props decide <if> at build time

In a component without a script, <if $icon> on a static prop is resolved by the compiler. The badge with icon ships the star inline and the other ships nothing, with no template and no runtime work. A bare attribute such as icon is true; icon="", icon="false" and a missing one are false.

What the compiler rejects

The list above is closed, so pragma check rejects what falls outside it, and every error names the fix:

  • The old API: :text (html/text-removed), export const state and actions, ctx.$, ctx.update and export function mount(ctx) (js/legacy-api).
  • Expressions in paths and in event arguments, {{ }} and ${ }, hand-written data-*, inline style and on*, :class, quoted block paths and a <for> without key.
  • Attributes from other frameworks, with the pragma form in the message: Vue's v-if, Alpine's x-show, Svelte's on:click, Angular's *ngIf, React's className.
  • Script mistakes that would show a stale value: data at the top level, a let derived from another let, a derived function used without () and $name in JS (State: script mistakes).

    Install

    pragma is one Rust binary. It compiles, checks, serves and bundles npm packages by itself: no Vite, no esbuild, no config. You need a Rust toolchain (cargo, from rustup) to build it. Node 22 or newer is needed only when an app has .server.js files, because pragma dev, pragma serve and the Node adapter run them.

    git clone https://github.com/leonavas/pragma
cd pragma
cargo install --path core/cli/crates/pragma-cli
     
    pragma -V

pragma — HTML, CSS and JS without a framework

usage:
  pragma new <dir>                              create an app in <dir> (empty or missing)
  pragma dev [--port 5180] [--host 127.0.0.1]   dev server with live reload
  pragma build                                  build dist/ for production
  pragma check [--strict]                       check HTML, CSS and JS (--strict: warnings become errors)
  pragma serve [--port 3000] [--host 127.0.0.1] serve dist/ as in production
  pragma upgrade                                update .pragma/ (runtime, docs, base.css, version) to this version
  pragma self-update [version]                  update the pragma CLI binary from GitHub Releases

  -V, --version   show the version

    Options take either form, --port 8080 or --port=8080. The cargo install output and the clone progress are left out above.

    To update, run git pull and the same cargo install, then pragma upgrade inside each app. It makes the app's .pragma/ (runtime, docs, base.css) match the new binary, prints every file it updated, added or removed, and never touches anything outside .pragma/. Until then pragma check warns with app/core-outdated.

    Create an app

    pragma new writes a working app into an empty or missing folder: a layout, a home page with a modal, an alert and a dropdown, a 404 page, the theme, the runtime in .pragma/ and the docs in .pragma/docs/.

    pragma new my-app
app created in my-app (41 files)

  cd my-app
  pragma dev

    The app ships an AGENTS.md (and a CLAUDE.md that includes it) with the syntax in a dozen lines, the rules the compiler enforces and a table that maps each task to one file in .pragma/docs/. A coding agent reads that first; you can too. The docs are short on purpose: every page fits in a context window.

    Your first component

    A component is a folder with one .html file: an optional <script>, the markup, an optional <style>. In the script, a top-level let is state, a function is an action when an event calls it and a derived value when the markup reads it, and export let declares a prop. In the markup, {$count} puts a value in the text, @click calls a function and :disabled binds an attribute. Assigning a variable is all it takes to update the page.

    Use it on any page. The build expands it in place, so its markup is in the prebuilt HTML, and its script loads only on pages that use it: a page with just this counter loads 8.9 kB of JS, runtime included.

    <c-counter label="Cups of coffee" start="1"></c-counter>
    • The default sets the prop's type: start="1" arrives as the number 1 because the default is 0; a bare attribute is true.
    • Props are read-only and live. let count = start copies one into state that the component can change.
    • The <style> is scoped with [data-c="counter"]; utilities from classes.md cover the rest.
    • pragma check reads the script: a name the markup uses but the script lacks is html/unknown-name, an attribute the component does not declare is html/unknown-prop, a write to a prop is js/prop-write.

    Project structure

    The layout is fixed, so there is nothing to configure and only one place for each thing. The files below are exactly what pragma new creates, minus .pragma/.

    pragma.json               name, lang and webmcp
AGENTS.md  CLAUDE.md      rules for coding agents
routes/
  _layout.html            header, footer, site-wide <head>; <slot> is the page
  _404.html               unknown URLs
  index.html              /         (markup, its <script> and <style>)
lib/
  components/<name>/      <c-name> for every page: modal, alert, dropdown
  state/<name>.js         stores, reached as shared.<name>
  theme.css               tokens and the few custom classes
utils/                    plain JS modules
public/                   copied as is: favicon.svg, images, fonts
.pragma/                  runtime and docs; never edited
    • Only routes/, lib/, utils/, .pragma/ and public/ are read. Other top-level files, like a README, are ignored.
    • A page is routes/x.html, with an optional <script> and <style> at its top level and an optional x.server.js (load, server actions, ssr). A large script can live in x.js beside it instead, never both (html/duplicate-module).
    • Anything else in routes/ must be private, with a leading underscore: _components/, _products.json, _catalog.server.js.
    • pragma.json takes exactly name (required: fallback title, log service name, Worker name), lang (default en) and webmcp (default true). Unknown keys are errors.

    The rules form a closed list. Anything outside the syntax is an error with a pointer to the fix, so an agent cannot quietly drift into another framework's habits.

    • JS: js/syntax, js/comment, js/console, js/vague-name, js/html-in-js (no innerHTML or createElement), js/jsdoc-types, js/import, and the script rules: js/component-script (no var, no top-level await, export only for props), js/prop-write, js/const-state (a mutated const the markup reads), js/store-import (stores only through shared) and js/legacy-api (the old state(ctx) API, with the migration).
    • HTML: html/syntax (close every non-void tag), html/comment, html/script, html/duplicate-module (a <script> and an x.js for the same file), html/style-inline, html/on-inline, html/legacy-syntax, html/unknown-directive, html/invalid-path, html/invalid-root, the block rules (html/block, html/for-without-key, html/misplaced-else…), html/unknown-name, html/unknown-prop, html/component, html/unknown-component, html/layout, html/title, html/class (no :class), html/text-removed (no :text), html/interpolation (no {{ }} or ${ } outside <code>/<pre>), html/data-attribute (no hand-written data-*) and html/head (<meta> and <link> only at the top of a page or in the layout head). html/unknown-directive also names the pragma form for Vue, Alpine, Svelte, Angular and React attributes.
    • CSS: css/syntax, css/comment, css/unknown-class (only the utilities in classes.md and classes your CSS defines), css/arbitrary-value.
    • App: app/structure, app/route-conflict, app/package, app/pragma-json, and the warning app/core-outdated when .pragma/ differs from the installed binary.
    • Accessibility, checked on the expanded page with components inlined: img-alt, accessible-name, label, dialog-name, click-non-interactive, heading, single-h1, tabindex, duplicate-id, iframe-title, a-no-href. A bound attribute counts: :aria-label satisfies aria-label.

    Performance

    pragma build prints the JS each page loads, gzip, runtime included, and the CSS size. The numbers are information only: no limit fails the build.

    A page with no script of its own costs 8.7 kB gzip, all of it runtime. When a page grows, make the code smaller. What the build does to keep pages small:

    • Every route is prebuilt HTML, and a page with a load starts its data fetch from an inline script in <head>, before any module runs.
    • Exactly the modules a page imports get a modulepreload. Modules are minified and hashed one by one; there is no app bundle.
    • The CSS contains only the classes the app uses.
    • Links prefetch on hover, focus or when visible; navigations use view transitions.
    • HTML is served no-cache, /assets/ as immutable, both brotli or gzip compressed.
    • Code needed only after a click goes behind await import() in the action: not preloaded, not in the page size. See lazy packages.

    Under the hood

    Nothing here needs configuring, but it helps when you read the built HTML or debug a deploy.

    • The generated <head> comes in this order: charset, viewport, <title>, the layout's head tags (a page's own <meta> and <link> replace the layout's tag with the same name), the theme script when used, the stylesheet, the inline /_data fetch when the page has a load, the modulepreloads, the route JSON and the boot module.
    • The route JSON, a <script> with id="pragma-route", tells the runtime what to start: 
      {"pattern":"/orders","page":null,"components":{},"stores":{},"loader":true,"ssr":false}
    • /_pragma/manifest.json lists every route with its HTML file, modules, loader and SSR flag. The client router and the Node adapter both read it.
    • Data travels as GET /_data/<path> and server actions as POST /_action/<path>/<name>, both with a traceparent header.
    • Not in v0: static generation with data, catch-all routes ([...rest]), per-route CSS, i18n and Speculation Rules.

Hand it to your agent

Nobody argues about frameworks anymore. The agent picks one.

Most people who build with an LLM don't know frontend. They ask for React or Angular because those are the names they know, and ship slow pages.

Some don't care and get plain HTML and JavaScript. Nothing beats it on speed. Nothing about it scales: it eats context, turns into a tangle, and the agent loses the thread.

Some know a bit more and pick SvelteKit, Astro or htmx. Good tools, made for people who read docs.

pragma is made for the agent:

  • The minimum lint that stops the tangle: one way to do each thing, and every error names the rule and the fix.
  • Components and reactivity on what the browser already has: ES modules, <template>, <dialog>, popover, view transitions.
  • One Rust binary compiles, lints and validates. No Vite, no config.
  • Plain JavaScript. Never TypeScript.
  • WebMCP by default: every form is a tool an agent in the browser can call. A page with a .md next to it answers in markdown when an agent asks.

One file: markup, script and style

A component is one .html file. A top-level let is state, a function is an action or a derived value, and {path} puts a value in the text. Check a task, add one, hide the done ones: each action assigns a variable and the runtime reapplies the bindings. No hooks, no virtual DOM. The form is also a WebMCP tool: an agent in the browser can call add_task.

Native

A page or a component is one .html file: the markup, its <script> and its <style>. Its data comes from the .server.js with the same name. No JSX, no virtual DOM, no framework between you and the platform.
